Five classmates are planning their class booth for the school festival in a group chat.

**Hana:** Our class meeting is tomorrow, so let's decide what booth to run. Last year we did a haunted house, but the science club is doing one this year, so we should pick something different.

**Riku:** I vote for a takoyaki stand. Food sells well, but the problem is we'd need a teacher to supervise the cooking, and Mr. Sato already told me he can't stay after 3 p.m.

**Mei:** The festival runs until 5 p.m., so a food stand that closes early would lose its busiest hours. How about a board-game café instead? No cooking, no supervision rules, and we already own most of the games.

**Riku:** I like that, but a café needs a lot of tables. The art club booked the big room with tables. We'd be stuck in a small classroom.

**Hana:** Actually, a small room is fine for a quiet café. My worry is money — we only have a 6,000-yen budget, and new games cost a lot.

**Mei:** We don't need new ones. I can bring six games from home, and Riku has three. That's enough to start.

**Daiki:** Then let's go with the board-game café. I'll make the sign and a price list tonight. Hana, can you ask our homeroom teacher to reserve the small classroom before someone else takes it?

**Hana:** Sure, I'll email her right after dinner. Mei, please bring your games to school on Friday so we can test them.

**Yuki:** Great. I'll count how many chairs the small room has and report back tomorrow.
question_data.subject: 英語

questions.stem: Why does the group decide against running a food stand?
choices: Because the science club is already selling food at the festival
Because the festival ends before the busiest selling hours begin
Because no teacher can supervise the cooking for the full festival hours
Because the class budget is too small to buy any cooking ingredients
questions.explanation: 正解は「Because no teacher can supervise the cooking for the full festival hours」。Riku は "we'd need a teacher to supervise the cooking, and Mr. Sato already told me he can't stay after 3 p.m." と述べ、Mei が "The festival runs until 5 p.m., so a food stand that closes early would lose its busiest hours" と続ける。つまり監督できるのが3時までで5時までの開催に足りないことが断念理由。科学部は怪奇屋敷(haunted house)であり食べ物ではないので他の選択肢は誤り。

choices: That the small classroom would be too quiet for customers
That the art club has already taken all the tables
That no teacher would agree to supervise the booth
That buying new board games would cost too much money
questions.explanation: 正解は「That buying new board games would cost too much money」。Hana は "My worry is money — we only have a 6,000-yen budget, and new games cost a lot." と明言している。テーブル不足を心配したのは Riku、静かな小部屋については Hana 自身が "a small room is fine" と問題視していないため、他は誤り。

Mei: I just remembered — I have a dentist appointment Saturday morning and can't take the bus. Coach said it's okay if I come by train and arrive at the lodge by noon. Is anyone else doing that?

Riku: No, I'll take the bus. But I can send you the lodge map, Mei, so you don't get lost from the station.

Mei: That would really help, thanks Riku!

**NOTICE: Changes to Library Rules — From July 1**

Hello, students! The Greenfield High School Library is making some changes from July 1. Please read this notice carefully before your next visit.

**Opening hours.** Until now, the library closed at 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. From July, it will stay open until 6:00 p.m. on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays so that students who join after-school clubs can still use it. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, the library will close at the usual time of 4:30 p.m. The Saturday morning hours (9:00 a.m.–12:00 noon) will not change.

**Borrowing.** You used to be able to borrow up to three books for two weeks. Now you may borrow up to five books, but the loan period is shorter: one week. If you need a book longer, you can renew it once online from the library website. You cannot renew a book that another student has already reserved.

**Eating and drinking.** Food is still not allowed anywhere in the library. However, students may now bring a drink in a bottle with a lid into the Reading Corner only. Drinks are still not allowed near the computers.

**Returning books.** A new return box has been placed outside the main door. You may drop books there at any time, even when the library is closed. Books left in the old box inside the library will no longer be collected.

If you have any questions, please ask Ms. Carter at the front desk.
question_data.subject: 英語

choices: Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays

Every weekday
Saturdays only

**Greenfield Park Cleanup — Volunteers Wanted!**

Greenfield Park needs your help! After last month's summer festival, our park is covered in litter, and the river path has become muddy and overgrown. Join the **Greenfield Community Cleanup** and help bring our park back to life.

**When:** Saturday, July 18, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. (rain date: Sunday, July 19)
**Where:** Meet at the East Gate, next to the parking lot.

Volunteers will be divided into three teams:
- **River Team** — clears weeds and trash along the muddy river path (boots provided; long sleeves and trousers required)
- **Garden Team** — plants flowers and waters the flower beds near the playground
- **Sorting Team** — separates collected items into recyclable and non-recyclable trash at the East Gate

You may choose your team when you sign up online by July 14. If you do not choose, we will place you in the team that needs the most people. **Students under 15 must bring an adult.**

Gloves, trash bags, and bottled water are free for everyone. Please wear clothes that can get dirty, and bring a hat and sunscreen. We will **not** provide lunch, so eat before you come or bring your own.

Everyone who finishes the morning will receive a "Green Helper" certificate, and the local café will give each volunteer a coupon for a free drink. Sign up at www.greenfieldpark.org/clean. Let's make Greenfield shine again!

**Greenwood High School — Library Committee Members Wanted!**

Do you love books and want to help your school? The Greenwood High School Library is looking for new student committee members for this year. No special experience is needed — just bring your energy and a friendly smile!

**What committee members do:**
- Help students find and borrow books at the front desk (Monday to Thursday, after school)
- Put returned books back on the shelves and keep the reading corner tidy
- Plan one "Book Week" event each term to get more students reading

**When and where to apply:**
Come to the library on Friday, May 8, between 3:30 p.m. and 5:00 p.m. Ms. Tanaka, the school librarian, will explain the job and answer your questions. You do not need to sign up before this meeting — just come on the day.

**Important points:**
- You must be free at least one afternoon a week. Members who join the front desk team work in pairs, so you will never be alone.
- First-year students are welcome, but you will need a short note from a parent. Second- and third-year students do not need this note.
- If you cannot come on May 8 but still want to join, send an email to Ms. Tanaka by May 15. She will arrange another time to meet you.

We hope to see many of you on May 8. Reading is more fun when we share it!

**Greenwood Hall Dining Survey Results**

Greenwood Hall, one of the largest student dormitories at Maple State University, runs a shared dining hall that serves breakfast and dinner to about 400 residents every day. Last month, the dormitory management team asked all residents to complete an online survey about the dining hall. A total of 312 students replied. The management posted the following summary on the dormitory website so that residents could see the results and decide what to improve first.

When asked how satisfied they were with the dining hall overall, 38% of students said they were "very satisfied," 41% said they were "somewhat satisfied," and the remaining 21% said they were "not satisfied." Students were also asked to choose the single area they most wanted the dining hall to improve. The most common answer was "more vegetarian and vegan choices" (34%), followed by "longer opening hours" (29%), "lower prices" (22%), and "better seating space" (15%). In a separate question, 67% of students said they ate at the dining hall at least five times a week, while only 9% said they almost never used it. Based on these numbers, the management announced that, starting next term, the dinner service would stay open one hour later and that two new plant-based main dishes would be added to the weekly menu. The management also noted that prices would not change for now, because the dining hall already runs at a small loss. To explain the results in more detail, two residents agreed to share their personal comments.

**Daniel (second-year student):**
I eat dinner at Greenwood almost every night because I have practice until late and cooking in my room is impossible. I am really happy about the new hours because I belong to the soccer team, and our practice ends at six o'clock. Before, the library was already closed by the time I finished, so I had to study at home, where my younger brothers are always noisy. Now I can stay and concentrate until eight. The one thing I am not sure about is the new rule for the study rooms. Last week I wanted a quiet room right after practice, but I could not book one because I forgot to reserve it the day before. I think students should be able to reserve a room on the same day if there are empty seats.

Lisa (Grade 12):
The longer evening hours are not very useful for me because I go to a cram school three evenings a week and have to leave school early. What I really wanted was for the library to open earlier in the morning, since I like to review my lessons before class. Opening at nine instead of eight actually makes my mornings harder. However, I am glad the library is finally open on Saturdays. I live far from any public library, so having a place to study near home on weekends will be a big help for me before the university entrance exams.

Your student council is reviewing the school's uniform policy. Last month, the council posted the following notice and survey results on the school website, along with two student comments.

NOTICE FROM THE STUDENT COUNCIL
Thank you to everyone who answered our online survey about the school uniform. We received responses from 480 students in all three grades. The council will present these results to the school board next week. Here is what we found.

We asked, "Should students be allowed to choose between a uniform and free clothing?" In response, 62% answered "yes," 25% answered "no," and 13% answered "not sure." We also asked which single change students most wanted. The most popular answer, chosen by 41%, was permission to wear the school's sports jacket on cold days. The second most popular, at 33%, was a free choice of trousers or a skirt regardless of gender. Only 9% asked for a completely new uniform design.

When we asked students to give one reason for keeping the uniform, the most common reason written in was "it saves time in the morning." When we asked for one reason against it, the most common was "the fabric is uncomfortable in summer." The council has not yet decided what to recommend; we will hold an open meeting on July 3 before writing our final report.

Comment from Mei (Grade 11):
I voted to keep the uniform, but I still think it needs changes. Last winter I was often cold because we are not allowed to wear our sports jacket in the hallways, even when the heating is weak. A friend of mine caught a cold in January, and she blamed the thin blazer. I am glad that wearing the sports jacket was the change most students wanted, because that shows I am not alone. I do not want to throw the uniform away. I just want a sensible rule that lets us stay warm and healthy.

Comment from Daniel (Grade 12):
Honestly, I think the survey question was unfair. Asking "uniform or free clothing" makes it sound like an all-or-nothing choice, so people who only wanted small changes had to pick a side. I would have preferred questions about each specific item. Also, I doubt 480 replies really speak for the whole school of over 1,200 students. I am not against keeping a uniform, and I actually like how it looks. My worry is only that the council may treat these numbers as the final voice of every student, when in fact many never replied at all.

I come to the gym almost every evening after work, so the crowded weight room is a real problem for me. Many times I have waited twenty minutes just to use one machine, which is frustrating after a long day. I think buying new running machines is a smart first step, but honestly, running machines are not what the evening crowd fights over — we all want the weight machines. I hope the center will count how many people actually wait each evening before deciding that six running machines are enough. The booking system sounds useful, though I worry some members will reserve a machine and then not come.

I mainly use the pool, and I am very happy that the water will finally be warmer in winter. Last January I stopped swimming for three weeks because the water was simply too cold for me. What I value most about this gym, however, is the price. My old gym charged almost double, so keeping the fee the same is the best news in this notice. I would gladly pay a little more if it meant longer pool hours on weekends, but I understand that many members are on a tight budget. The new booking system may help the pool too, since the lanes also get busy on Sunday mornings.

Last spring, I had an experience that changed the way I think about kindness.

It was a rainy Saturday morning, and I was on my way to the city library to return some books. Because the train was crowded, I had to stand near the door, holding my heavy bag with both hands. When the train reached my station, I rushed out so quickly that I did not notice something fall from my pocket. I only realized it after I had walked up the stairs and reached the ticket gate. When I checked my pocket, my train pass was gone. My face turned pale. The pass was not only expensive but also held a small photo of my grandmother inside the case, and that photo meant a lot to me.

I ran back down to the platform, but of course the train had already left. I felt like crying. A station worker told me kindly that lost items are sometimes brought to the office, but he could not promise anything. I left my name and phone number and went home, feeling heavy and sad all day.

Three days later, on Tuesday afternoon, my phone rang. It was the station office. A high school girl had found my pass on the train floor and handed it to a worker at the next station. When I went to pick it up, the worker gave me a short note. The girl had written, "I saw the photo inside and thought someone must be missing this. I hope it finds its way home." She had not left her name, only those words. Holding the note, I felt warm tears in my eyes.

That evening, I decided I wanted to do something similar for someone else. The very next morning, while waiting for the bus, I saw a wallet lying on the bench beside me. Remembering the girl's kindness, I picked it up at once and took it to the nearest police box. The officer thanked me and said the owner would be very relieved. As I walked away, I felt lighter than I had in days.

Looking back now, I understand that the girl gave me more than my pass. She showed me that a small act of care can travel from one stranger to another, like a gift passed quietly from hand to hand. I never learned her name, but I think of her often, especially on rainy mornings. Now, whenever I find something that someone has lost, I do not hesitate. I simply pass the kindness along, hoping it will keep moving forward.

When I was eleven, I could not swim at all. Every summer my friends went to the city pool, but I always stayed home because I was afraid of deep water. One afternoon in June, my older cousin Mika visited us. She had been a member of her school swimming team, and when she heard about my fear, she smiled and said, "By the end of August, you will swim across the pool. I promise."

The next morning, she took me to the pool early, before it became crowded. At first, I would not even put my face in the water. Mika did not laugh at me. Instead, she sat on the edge with me and showed me how to blow bubbles. We practiced only that for the whole first day. It felt silly, but slowly I stopped feeling so nervous.

After about a week, I could put my whole head under the water and open my eyes. Then Mika taught me how to float on my back. This was the hardest part for me. Whenever I tried, I was sure I would sink, so my body became stiff and I went straight down. Mika kept one hand under my back and told me to relax and breathe slowly. "The water wants to hold you," she said. "You just have to trust it." One quiet morning, she quietly took her hand away, and I floated alone for almost ten seconds. I was so surprised that I stood up and shouted with joy.

Once I could float, learning to move was easier than I had expected. Mika showed me how to kick my legs and pull the water with my arms. We practiced near the wall so I could grab it if I felt tired. Day by day, I swam a little farther. Some days I swallowed water and wanted to quit, but Mika always reminded me how far I had already come.

Finally, on the last Saturday of August, Mika stood at the far end of the pool and called my name. I pushed off from the wall and swam toward her without stopping. When my hand touched the wall on the other side, I could not believe it. I had crossed the whole pool by myself. Mika hugged me and said she had never doubted me for a moment.

That summer taught me something I will never forget. The thing I feared most became the thing I loved most. Now, whenever a new challenge looks too big, I remember the feeling of floating alone on the water, and I tell myself to trust, relax, and keep going.

Last summer, I played in the regional badminton tournament for my high school. I had practiced for months, but on the morning of the match, my hands felt cold and my heart would not stop racing. I am usually a calm person, yet that day I could not even tie my shoes properly. My doubles partner, Kenta, noticed and gave me a small smile, but I was too nervous to smile back.

When we arrived at the gym, the noise of the crowd hit me like a wave. There were hundreds of people in the seats, and the bright lights made the court look enormous. I remember thinking, "Everyone is watching. What if I make a mistake?" My legs felt heavy, and I wanted to sit down in a corner and hide. Kenta must have seen my pale face, because he walked over and said quietly, "Just breathe. We've done this a thousand times in practice. Today is no different." His calm words did not magically fix my fear, but they reminded me that I was not alone.

Our first match began at ten o'clock. In the opening minutes, I missed three easy shots in a row. My hands were shaking, and I could feel my face turning red. The other team scored point after point, and soon we were losing badly. During a short break, our coach, Ms. Mori, knelt beside me. Instead of scolding me, she said, "Stop thinking about the score. Watch the shuttlecock, and trust your body." I closed my eyes, took a long breath, and tried to forget the crowd completely.

Something changed after that. When the match restarted, I stopped worrying about the audience and focused only on each shot, one at a time. Slowly, my movements became smoother, and my old confidence returned. Kenta and I began to work together as we always had in practice, calling out to each other and covering the court. We did not win that first match, but we lost by only two points, and I no longer felt afraid.

By the afternoon, I was a different player. In our second match, my hands were steady and my mind was clear. We won easily, and as I shook hands with our opponents, I realized something important. The crowd had not disappeared, and my fear had not vanished forever. What had changed was me: I had learned to act despite my nervousness instead of waiting for it to go away. That lesson, I think, was worth far more than any trophy.

question_data.passage:
Eco Week at Sakura High: A Report from the Environment Club

Last month, our Environment Club held its first-ever Eco Week, and I would like to share what we did and what we learned. When we first proposed the idea to our teachers, some of them were not sure that students would really (1) participate, because earlier club events had drawn small crowds. <A> However, the response surprised everyone. By Friday, more than three hundred students had joined at least one of our activities, which was far more than we had hoped for.

We planned a different theme for each day. On Monday, we set up a "second-hand book corner" in the library, where students could leave books they no longer needed and take ones they wanted to read. <B> On Tuesday, we ran a workshop on making small bags from old T-shirts, and the sewing room was full all afternoon. On Wednesday, members of the science club measured how much electricity the school uses each day and explained simple ways to reduce it, such as turning off classroom lights during lunch. <C>

Thursday was the busiest day. We asked the cafeteria to weigh the food that students threw away, and the result shocked us. In a single lunch, our school produced almost forty kilograms of food waste. When we showed this number on a large poster, many students said they had never imagined the total could be so high. <D> On Friday, we asked everyone to bring a reusable bottle instead of buying drinks in plastic ones, and the number of plastic bottles in the recycling bins dropped sharply compared with a normal day.

Of course, (2) not everything went smoothly. The weather on Wednesday was rainy, so the outdoor garden activity had to move indoors at the last minute, and some students went home before they found the new room. We also realized that one week is too short to change daily habits. Still, the feedback we collected was encouraging. Several students wrote that they had started carrying their own bottles even after Eco Week ended, and two teachers asked us to repeat the food-waste survey next term.

Looking back, I think the most valuable lesson was not about the environment itself but about people. We learned that (3) students will take action when they can see a clear reason to do so. A poster with a shocking number changed more behavior than any long speech could have. For our club, Eco Week was therefore not only an event but also (4) a turning point. We now have many new members and a clear plan for the future.

Comments:
(1) Add words after the underline that explain why the teachers doubted students.
(2) This phrase introduces the problems the club faced. Make sure the example that follows matches it.
(3) The underlined sentence is a bit weak. Replace it with a clearer statement of your main finding.
(4) Choose words that summarize the overall meaning of Eco Week for the club.
question_data.subject: 英語

question_data.passage:
You are a member of the library committee at your high school. One of your classmates, Mei, has written a draft to introduce the school's upcoming Reading Week. Your teacher, Ms. Carter, has read the draft and left comments. Read the draft and the comments, and help Mei improve her writing.

Mei's draft:

Welcome to Reading Week!

Every November, our school library holds a special event called Reading Week. This year it will run from Monday, November 16, to Friday, November 20. The library committee has been planning it since September, and we are excited to finally share the details with you. <A> Reading Week is not only for students who already love books. (1) It is also for those who have never thought of reading as fun, because we have prepared activities that anyone can enjoy.

The main event is the "Book Exchange Corner." If you bring a book you have already read and no longer need, you can swap it for a book that another student has brought. <B> Last year, more than two hundred books were exchanged in a single week, and many students told us they discovered authors they had never heard of before. (2) We expect this year to be even more successful, since the number of students taking part has grown steadily.

We will also hold daily "Lunchtime Talks." Each day, a different teacher will speak for ten minutes about a book that changed the way they think. <C> The talks are short, so you can drop in during lunch without missing your meal. We hope these talks will show you that reading is not a lonely activity but something we can share and discuss together.

Finally, do not forget the "Reading Passport." Every time you borrow a book during Reading Week, a librarian will stamp your passport. <D> Students who collect five stamps will receive a small bookmark designed by our art club. The point is not the prize itself; rather, the passport is meant to encourage you to keep coming back to the library.

So please join us. Whether you read one page or one hundred, Reading Week is a chance to (3) make reading a habit you carry beyond a single week. We look forward to seeing you in the library!

Comments:

(1) Good start, but the sentence stops too suddenly. Add a phrase that completes your point about who Reading Week is for.

(2) This is a strong claim. Replace this sentence with one that supports your expectation using the evidence you already mentioned, rather than just repeating the claim.

(3) You want to leave readers with your main message. Choose the phrase that best captures the overall purpose of Reading Week as described in your draft.

Insertion: You also have one extra sentence that you cut earlier. Decide where it fits best: "No special skill is needed; you only have to be willing to try."

次の1文を入れるのに最も適切な位置を <A>〜<D> から選びなさい。
挿入文: "No special skill is needed; you only have to be willing to try."
questions.explanation: 正解は「<A>」。挿入文は「特別な技能は要らず、やってみる気持ちさえあればよい」という、参加への敷居の低さを述べる一般的な内容。<A> の直後では「Reading Week は本好きの生徒だけのものではなく、読書を楽しいと思ったことのない生徒にも向けたものだ」と参加対象の広さを説明しており、挿入文はその導入として自然につながる。<B><C><D> はそれぞれ Book Exchange・Lunchtime Talks・Reading Passport という具体的な活動の説明の途中であり、技能不要という一般論を挟むと話の流れが途切れて不自然になる。

choices: turn reading into a lasting part of your daily life

win the bookmark prize before anyone else does
avoid going to the library after Reading Week ends

Thank you for coming today. Our club has been preparing for this event for almost three months, and we are excited to share what we have learned. This guide will help you (1)make the most of, so please keep it with you as you walk around.

There are a few things we would like you to remember. Please do not touch the displays unless a sign says you may, because (2)some of the experiments are still running and a small change could ruin a whole week of work. If you have a question, look for a student wearing a yellow badge; they are happy to explain anything. (3)We would be glad if you ask us many questions, and we think it is a good thing to do.

At noon, the winners of the poster contest will be announced in the main hall. Voting closes at 11:30, so be sure to choose your favourite poster before then. Each visitor may vote only once.

We hope you enjoy your visit. (4)Science is fun, and we made this fair to share it.

Comments:
(1) You started this sentence but did not finish it. "Make the most of" needs an object. Add words so the sentence is complete and natural.
(2) This underlined part is fine, but please look at the sentence that follows the plant experiments. I want to add the sentence "Some of these were planted by elementary school children who visit us each spring." Where in the second paragraph should it go? Choose the best position from <A>, <B>, <C>, and <D>.

Please feel free to ask us as many questions as you like.
We would be glad, and we think asking many questions is good.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Please feel free to ask us as many questions as you like.」。元の文 "We would be glad if you ask us many questions, and we think it is a good thing to do." は「質問してくれたら嬉しい」と「良いことだと思う」という同じ主旨を二度繰り返して冗長。これを一文の丁寧な依頼にまとめた選択肢が最適で、来場者に質問を促す本来の意図を簡潔に伝える。選択肢2は主語が We(来場者でなく自分たちが質問する)になり意味が逆転、選択肢3は同語反復で文法も崩壊、選択肢4は元文の冗長な二重表現をほぼそのまま残しており指摘に応えていない。

questions.stem: Comment (4) asks for a stronger closing sentence to replace underlined part (4). Which best states the writers' main message?
choices: Thank you again for coming to the Greenhill High School Science Fair today.
Science is sometimes difficult, but you should try your best to understand it.
We made this fair in three months, so please look at every single display.
We hope today sparks your own curiosity and shows you that science belongs to everyone.
questions.explanation: 正解は「We hope today sparks your own curiosity and shows you that science belongs to everyone.」。下書き全体は来場者に科学を体験して楽しんでもらうことを目的としており、最後の "Science is fun, and we made this fair to share it."(科学は楽しい・それを分かち合うために開いた)を、より力強く主旨を述べる文に置き換える。来場者の好奇心を刺激し「科学は皆のもの」と伝える選択肢が、楽しさと共有という本来のメッセージを最も強く言い換えている。選択肢2は努力を求める別の主旨にすり替わり、選択肢3は準備期間という枝葉に焦点を移し、選択肢4は単なる礼で主張が無く『flat(平板)』という指摘を解消していない。

question_data.passage:
You are a member of the book club at Greenfield High School. The club is organizing a charity book fair, and you find the leaflet below on the club's notice board.

--- LEAFLET ---

Greenfield High School Charity Book Fair — "Pass It On"

Saturday, July 18, 10:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m. in the School Gymnasium

This year, students sell used books they love so that others can enjoy them. All money goes to the Greenfield Children's Library, which buys new books for kids in our town.

How to take part as a seller:
- Choose up to FIVE books you have read and want to pass on.
- Fill in one Recommendation Form for EACH book and submit all forms by Friday, July 3.
- Write a short comment so buyers can decide. Forms with no comment will be returned to you.
- Set a price between 100 and 500 yen. Books in the "Classics" group may be priced higher, up to 800 yen.
- We cannot accept textbooks, magazines, or any book published this year.

On the fair day, books will be displayed by GROUP, not by seller. Visitors can read your comment before they buy. Thank you for passing your favorite stories on to a younger reader!

--- RECOMMENDATION FORMS (submitted by club members) ---

Form 1
Seller: Mika
Title: The Silent Forest
Author: Helen Carter
Group: Mystery
Price: 300 yen
Comment: I read this twice. The ending surprised me both times, and I still think about it.

Form 2
Seller: Daniel
Title: Voices of the Sea
Author: Robert Lane
Group: Classics
Price: 700 yen
Comment: My grandfather gave me this old novel. The language is a little difficult, but the story of a fishing village stayed with me.

Form 3
Seller: Mika
Title: Cooking for Beginners
Author: Sophie Bell
Group: Hobby
Price: 250 yen
Comment: (blank)

Form 4
Seller: Aiko
Title: The Long Road Home
Author: James Wood
Group: Adventure
Price: 400 yen
Comment: A boy walks across a country to find his family. I could not stop turning the pages on a rainy weekend.

Form 5
Seller: Daniel
Title: Numbers and You
Author: Greenfield Math Dept.
Group: Hobby
Price: 200 yen
Comment: This is the math textbook our school used last year. It helped me a lot before exams.

--- EMAIL FROM THE ORGANIZER ---

From: Ms. Porter (Book Club Adviser)
To: All sellers
Date: July 6
Subject: Two quick things before the fair

Hello everyone,

Thank you for your forms. The fair is going to be wonderful. Before we print the price labels, I need to fix two problems.

First, one form cannot be accepted in its current state because the rules clearly say what every book needs in order to go on the table. Please send me the missing part by July 8, or that book will not be displayed.

Second, one book has been placed in a group that does not fit what the book actually is, so I will move it to the correct group myself — no action is needed from you for that one.

I also have a request for two of you. Mika and Aiko, could each of you bring one large box on the fair day? We need boxes to carry the unsold books back to the club room, and yours are the books most likely to attract many buyers, so your tables will empty fastest. Daniel, please arrive 30 minutes early to help set up the Classics corner.

See you on July 18!

Ms. Porter

questions.stem: Which combination correctly describes two of the submitted forms?
choices: Daniel's Classics book is the most expensive, and Aiko's adventure book costs more than Mika's mystery book.
Mika's mystery book is the cheapest, and Daniel's Classics book is the most expensive.
Aiko's adventure book is the cheapest, and Mika's hobby book is the most expensive.
Mika's mystery book costs the same as Daniel's hobby book, and both are Classics.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Daniel's Classics book is the most expensive, and Aiko's adventure book costs more than Mika's mystery book.」。価格はDaniel(Voices of the Sea, Classics)700円が最高、Aiko(The Long Road Home)400円>Mika(The Silent Forest)300円で正しい。最安はDanielのNumbers and You 200円なのでMikaのミステリーが最安とする選択肢は誤り。

questions.stem: Based on the leaflet's rules, which book among the submitted forms is NOT allowed to be sold at the fair at all?
choices: The Silent Forest by Helen Carter
Numbers and You by the Greenfield Math Dept.
The Long Road Home by James Wood
Voices of the Sea by Robert Lane
questions.explanation: 正解は「Numbers and You by the Greenfield Math Dept.」。リーフレットは「We cannot accept textbooks」と明記し、Form 5のDanielのコメントに「This is the math textbook our school used last year」とある。これは教科書なので販売自体が不可。他3冊はルール違反がない。

questions.stem: In her email, Ms. Porter asks the sellers to do two things. Which combination correctly states what she requests?
choices: Daniel must add a missing comment, and Mika must arrive 30 minutes early.
Aiko must change her book's group, and Daniel must bring a large box.
Mika must add a missing comment, and she and Aiko must each bring a large box.
Mika must change her book's group, and Daniel must arrive 30 minutes early.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Mika must add a missing comment, and she and Aiko must each bring a large box.」。コメント欄が空(blank)なのはMikaのForm 3で、メールの「send me the missing part by July 8」が指すのはこの本。さらに「Mika and Aiko, could each of you bring one large box」と箱を依頼している。グループ変更はMs. Porter自身が行うとあり生徒の作業は不要、早く来るのはDaniel。

question_data.passage:
You are planning to take part in a community activity. You found a leaflet, a filled-in entry form, and an email about it.

=== RESOURCE 1: LEAFLET ===

GREENFIELD COMMUNITY GARDEN — "GROW & SHARE" FESTIVAL

The Greenfield Community Garden invites you to our biggest event of the year! For the past six years, neighbors have come together to grow vegetables and flowers on land that was once an empty parking lot. This summer, we want to celebrate what we have grown and share it with everyone in town.

When: Saturday, August 22nd, 10:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m.
Where: Greenfield Garden, behind the public library

At the festival, members will display the plants they have grown in their own garden beds. Visitors can taste fresh vegetables, learn how to start a garden at home, and buy young plants to take away. If you want to display your plants, please fill in the entry form below.

Rules for displaying plants:
- Each member may display up to three plants.
- Every plant must have been grown in our garden this year. Plants bought from a shop are not allowed.
- Plants for sale must be priced between $2 and $8. Plants that are only for display (not for sale) do not need a price.
- Vegetables, flowers, and herbs are all welcome. We cannot accept trees.
- Please write a short comment so visitors can learn about each plant.

The member whose plant gets the most visitor votes will win a free gardening workshop in September. Only plants that are for sale can take part in the voting.

=== RESOURCE 2: ENTRY FORM (filled in by a member) ===

Name: Daniel Park    Garden Bed Number: 14

| Plant | Type | For Sale? | Price | My Comment |
|-------|------|-----------|-------|------------|
| Sungold Tomato | Vegetable | Yes | $6 | These small tomatoes are very sweet. My children eat them like candy! |
| Lavender | Flower/Herb | Yes | $4 | I planted this in spring. Its smell helps me relax after a long day. |
| Giant Pumpkin | Vegetable | No | — | This is the biggest thing I have ever grown. I want to show it, not sell it. |

=== RESOURCE 3: EMAIL FROM THE ORGANIZER ===

From: Maria Lopez, Festival Team
To: Daniel Park
Subject: Your entry — almost ready!

Dear Daniel,

Thank you for your entry. We are happy that you are joining the festival again. I have checked your form, and I have two small requests before the big day.

First, your Sungold Tomato and your Lavender are both fine, and they will be part of the visitor voting. Your Giant Pumpkin will be displayed next to the entrance so that everyone can see it as they arrive, but please remember it cannot win the workshop prize.

Second, could you bring a few photos showing how these plants grew from seed to now? We would like to put them on a board so visitors can understand the whole process. Also, we still need helpers to welcome visitors at the gate from 9:30 a.m. Could you arrive thirty minutes early and help us greet people before we open? Many hands make the morning easier.

Please reply by August 15th to let me know about the photos and the early help. If you cannot come early, that is no problem — just tell me so we can ask another member.

Warm wishes,
Maria

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the leaflet (Resource 1)?
choices: To explain how the garden was built on an old parking lot
To announce the winner of this year's gardening workshop
To advertise a shop that sells young vegetables and flowers
To invite people to an event and to ask members to enter their plants
questions.explanation: 正解は「To invite people to an event and to ask members to enter their plants」。リーフレットは冒頭で「invites you to our biggest event of the year」と来場を呼びかけ、続けて「If you want to display your plants, please fill in the entry form below」と会員に出品(エントリ)を促している。駐車場の話は背景説明の一部にすぎず、ショップの宣伝や受賞発表ではない。

questions.stem: According to the leaflet, which plant would NOT be accepted at the festival?
choices: A small tree grown in the garden this year and offered for sale at $7
A flower grown in the garden this year shown only for display with no price
A herb grown in the garden this year and offered for sale at $5
A vegetable grown in the garden this year and offered for sale at $3
questions.explanation: 正解は「A small tree grown in the garden this year and offered for sale at $7」。リーフレットのルールに「Vegetables, flowers, and herbs are all welcome. We cannot accept trees.」とあり、木は今年庭で育てたものでも受け付けられない。他の3つはハーブ・花・野菜で価格も$2〜$8の範囲内、または非売品の展示のみで、いずれもルールを満たす。

questions.stem: Which combination correctly describes two of Daniel's plants based on the form and the email?
choices: The Sungold Tomato and the Giant Pumpkin will both take part in the voting.
The Sungold Tomato and the Lavender will both take part in the voting.
The Lavender and the Giant Pumpkin are both priced for sale.
The Lavender and the Giant Pumpkin will both be placed by the entrance.
questions.explanation: 正解は「The Sungold Tomato and the Lavender will both take part in the voting.」。フォームではSungold TomatoとLavenderが「For Sale? Yes」で価格付き、メールでもMariaが「your Sungold Tomato and your Lavender are both fine, and they will be part of the visitor voting」と確認している。Giant Pumpkinは非売品(For Sale? No、価格は「—」)で、リーフレットの「Only plants that are for sale can take part in the voting」より投票対象外。よって他の組合せは誤り。

questions.stem: Why can Daniel's Giant Pumpkin NOT win the workshop prize?
choices: Because it was not grown in the Greenfield Garden this year
Because it will be placed at the entrance instead of inside
Because it is for display only and not for sale
Because Daniel has already entered three plants in total
questions.explanation: 正解は「Because it is for display only and not for sale」。フォームでGiant Pumpkinは「For Sale? No」「Price —」で展示のみ。リーフレットには「Only plants that are for sale can take part in the voting」「The member whose plant gets the most visitor votes will win a free gardening workshop」とあり、投票=賞の条件は「売り物であること」。非売品ゆえ投票に入れず賞も取れない。入口に置くこと自体や本数(3つは上限内)は理由ではない。

questions.stem: In the email, what two things does Maria ask Daniel to do?
choices: To lower the price of his plants and to bring extra young plants to sell
To remove the Giant Pumpkin from the entry and to reply after the festival
To vote for other members' plants and to arrive at 9:30 a.m. as a visitor
To bring photos of how the plants grew and to come early to help greet visitors
questions.explanation: 正解は「To bring photos of how the plants grew and to come early to help greet visitors」。メールの「Second」段落でMariaは「could you bring a few photos showing how these plants grew from seed to now?」と写真を依頼し、続けて「Could you arrive thirty minutes early and help us greet people before we open?」と早めの来場・受付の手伝いを頼んでいる。価格変更や苗の追加、投票依頼、出品の取り消しは述べられていない。

question_data.passage:
You are a second-year student at Sakura High School. Your class is preparing for a three-day school trip in October, and each student must choose one of four day-trip courses for the second day. Read the leaflet, the choice forms filled in by four students, and an email from the teacher in charge, and then answer the questions.

【Leaflet: Day 2 Course Guide】

Welcome to the Day 2 course selection! On the second day of our school trip, you will leave the hotel in the morning and spend the whole day on the course you choose. Buses return to the hotel by 6:00 p.m. Please read the four options carefully before you decide.

Course A: Mountain Hiking
Walk a 9-kilometer forest trail and enjoy the autumn leaves from the top of Mt. Aoba. A guide goes with each group. You need strong shoes and a raincoat. This course is not available if it rains, so people who choose it must also write a second choice.

Course B: City History Walk
Visit three old temples and a castle in the city center. A local volunteer explains the history of each place. There is a lot of walking on flat roads, so anyone can join. Lunch is eaten at a traditional restaurant near the castle.

Course C: Sea Kayaking
Paddle a kayak along the calm coast with an instructor. No experience is needed, but you must be able to swim 25 meters. All equipment is provided. Because of safety rules, each group can take only eight students.

Course D: Craft Workshop
Make your own cup at a pottery studio and paint it freely. The finished cup is sent to your home two weeks later. This is an indoor course, so the weather does not matter. The fee includes the cost of mailing.

Notes:
- The fee for each course is 2,000 yen, except Course C, which is 3,500 yen because of the boat and safety staff.
- Course A and Course C may be canceled for safety reasons. Course B and Course D run in any weather.
- Write your name, your first choice, and a short comment on the form.

【Choice Forms】

Form 1 — Name: Kenji
First choice: Course A
Second choice: Course D
Comment: I love walking in the mountains, and I want to see the red and yellow leaves. If the weather is bad, I would rather stay inside and make something with my hands.

Form 2 — Name: Mai
First choice: Course C
Second choice: (none)
Comment: I joined a kayak club last summer, so I am confident in the water. I can swim well, and I really want to try the sea here.

Form 3 — Name: Sota
First choice: Course B
Second choice: (none)
Comment: I hurt my knee in May, so I cannot do hard exercise yet. A walk on flat ground is fine, and I am interested in old buildings.

Form 4 — Name: Yuna
First choice: Course D
Second choice: (none)
Comment: I am not good at sports, and I get tired easily. I would like a calm, indoor day. I also like the idea of keeping something I made myself.

【Email from the teacher】

From: Mr. Tanaka (Trip Leader)
To: All Day 2 course members
Subject: Two things to check before Day 2

Hello, everyone. Thank you for sending your forms. I have checked them all, and most are fine. However, two students need to do something more.

First, Mai, you chose Course C but left the second-choice box empty. Course C may be canceled for safety reasons, so every member of that course must write a second choice in case it cannot run. Please send me your second choice by Friday.

Second, the safety office told me that Course C now has nine students who want to join, but each group can take only eight. So one student will have to move to another course. I will decide who moves by the order in which the forms arrived, and Mai's form was the last one. I am sorry, Mai. Please be ready for this.

To the others: there is nothing you need to change. Just remember to bring the right clothes for your course, and bring 2,000 yen, or 3,500 yen for Course C, on the morning of Day 2. See you soon.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the leaflet?
choices: To help students choose one course for the second day of the trip
To explain how students can change their hotel rooms during the trip
To advertise the city's temples and castle to tourists from other towns
To collect money for the school trip before the students leave home
questions.explanation: 正解は「To help students choose one course for the second day of the trip」。リーフレットの冒頭に「Welcome to the Day 2 course selection!」「Please read the four options carefully before you decide.」とあり、第2日の4つのコースから1つを選ぶための案内であることが目的だと分かる。ホテルの部屋や観光客向け宣伝、事前集金は本文の趣旨ではない。

questions.stem: According to the leaflet, which statement is true?
choices: Course C is the cheapest of the four courses because all equipment is free.
Course D's fee already covers the cost of sending the finished cup home.
Course A and Course D both continue even when it rains.
Course B requires students to be able to swim 25 meters before joining.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Course D's fee already covers the cost of sending the finished cup home.」。Course Dの説明に「The fee includes the cost of mailing.」とあり、完成したカップを家へ送る郵送費が料金に含まれると述べられている。Course Cは3,500円で最も高く(最安ではない)、雨で続くのはB・Dであり(Aは雨だと不可)、25メートル泳ぐ条件はBではなくCの要件なので、他は誤り。

questions.stem: Look at the forms. Which pair of students gave a reason that matches a course rule or feature stated in the leaflet?
choices: Kenji's reason for Course D and Mai's reason for Course C
Yuna's reason for Course A and Sota's reason for Course D
Sota's reason for Course B and Mai's reason for Course C
Kenji's reason for Course C and Yuna's reason for Course B
questions.explanation: 正解は「Sota's reason for Course B and Mai's reason for Course C」。Course Bは「a lot of walking on flat roads, so anyone can join」で、Sotaは膝のため激しい運動はできず平地歩行なら大丈夫と書いており規則に合致する。Course Cは「you must be able to swim 25 meters」で、Maiは「I can swim well」と泳力を述べており要件に合う。KenjiとYunaは実際にはDを希望(KenjiはAが第1・Dが第2)しており、選択肢のC・Aとの組合せは事実と合わない。

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT something the leaflet says about the courses?
choices: A guide or instructor goes with the students on Course A and Course C.
Course D is held indoors, so the weather does not affect it.
Course B includes lunch at a traditional restaurant near the castle.
Students on every course must write a second choice on their form.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Students on every course must write a second choice on their form.」。リーフレットで第2希望の記入を求めているのはCourse A(雨で中止になり得るため)だけで、全コースの参加者に義務付けてはいない。Aには「A guide goes with each group」、Cには「with an instructor」とあり、Dは「indoor course, so the weather does not matter」、Bは「Lunch is eaten at a traditional restaurant near the castle」とあるので、他の3つは本文に書かれている。

questions.stem: In the email, what does Mr. Tanaka ask Mai to do?
choices: Write a second choice and be ready to move to another course
Pay an extra fee for Course C and arrive earlier than the others
Bring her own kayak equipment and a second pair of shoes
Change her first choice to Course B and tell her friends about it
questions.explanation: 正解は「Write a second choice and be ready to move to another course」。メールでは、第1にMaiがCourse Cで第2希望欄を空けたため「Please send me your second choice by Friday.」と第2希望の記入を求め、第2にCが9人で定員8人を超え、到着順で最後だったMaiが「one student will have to move to another course」「Please be ready for this.」と移動の可能性に備えるよう伝えている。追加料金や早着、自前の用具持参、Bへの変更指示は述べられていない。

question_data.passage:
You are a member of the art club at Greenfield High School. You found this leaflet on the club's notice board and decided to apply. Below are the leaflet, the online form you filled in, and an email you later received from the organizer.

=== LEAFLET ===

GREENFIELD CITY ART MUSEUM
Student Volunteers Wanted for the Summer Art Show

This August, the Greenfield City Art Museum will hold its biggest event of the year, "Young Eyes," an exhibition of paintings created by local students. We are looking for high school students to help us run the show. No experience is needed, but you must enjoy talking with visitors.

There are four roles. Please choose one when you apply.
- Guide: walk around the gallery and answer visitors' questions about the paintings.
- Greeter: stand at the front door, welcome visitors, and hand out programs.
- Helper: set up and clean the rooms before and after each day.
- Reporter: take notes during the show and write a short article for our website.

Important conditions:
- You must be 15 years old or older by August 1.
- Guides and Reporters must come to a one-day training session on July 25. Greeters and Helpers do not need training.
- Every volunteer must work at least two days during the show (August 5-9).
- Reporters must be able to use a computer at home to write their article.

To apply, fill in the online form by July 10. We will email you within one week.

=== ONLINE FORM (your saved copy) ===

Name: Kenji Mori
Age (on August 1): 16
Role you want: Reporter
Days you can work: August 5, 6, 8
Comment: I write for my school newspaper, so I think I can do this job well. I have my own computer, and I would love to learn how museums plan an exhibition. I am a little worried because I have a family trip from August 9 in the evening, but I can work in the morning that day too if needed.

We also asked three friends to apply. Here is what they wrote.

Name: Aya Tanaka
Age (on August 1): 15
Role you want: Greeter
Days you can work: August 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
Comment: I love meeting new people and I am good at remembering faces. I cannot draw well, so I was happy to find a job that does not need art skills. I can come every single day of the show.

Name: Sho Yamada
Age (on August 1): 14
Role you want: Helper
Days you can work: August 7, 8, 9
Comment: I am strong and I do not mind carrying heavy things. My birthday is on August 10, so I will turn 15 right after the show. I hope that is okay.

Name: Rina Kato
Age (on August 1): 17
Role you want: Guide
Days you can work: August 5, 9
Comment: I have visited many art museums and I can explain paintings in an easy way. I can only come on the first and last days because of cram school on the other days.

=== EMAIL ===

From: Greenfield City Art Museum
To: Kenji Mori
Subject: About your application

Dear Kenji,

Thank you for applying to be a Reporter for "Young Eyes." We are glad to have you on the team. Your experience with the school newspaper will be very useful.

We have two small requests. First, please come to the training session on July 25 at 10:00. There you will meet the other Reporters and learn what to write about. Second, because you will leave on the evening of August 9, please send your finished article to us by August 12, three days after the show ends, so that we can put it on the website on time.

One more thing: we noticed that one of the friends you told us about cannot join this year. We will contact that person directly to explain the reason. The other two will receive emails like this one soon.

We look forward to seeing you in July.

Best wishes,
Ms. Carter
Event Organizer

questions.stem: Among the four people who filled in the form, who cannot become a volunteer this year?

Sho Yamada, because he is not old enough
Kenji Mori, because he has a family trip
Rina Kato, because she can only work two days

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches a role with a person who chose it?
choices: Aya chose the role that must attend the July 25 training.
Kenji chose the role that hands out programs at the front door.
Rina chose the role that answers visitors' questions in the gallery.
Sho chose the role that writes an article for the website.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Rina chose the role that answers visitors' questions in the gallery.」。Rina のフォームは「Role you want: Guide」で、リーフレットの Guide は「answer visitors' questions about the paintings」と一致する。Aya は Greeter(研修不要。研修が必要なのは Guides と Reporters)。Kenji は Reporter で、プログラムを配るのは Greeter の仕事。Sho は Helper で、記事を書くのは Reporter の仕事。役割と人物がずれている他の3つは誤り。

questions.stem: Which is NOT something the leaflet lists as a condition for volunteers?
choices: Working at least two days during August 5-9
Being 15 or older by August 1

You are in an English class. Read the following story and complete the Story Outline below.

The Corner Bakery

Mr. Tani had run a small bakery at the entrance of the shopping street for almost forty years. He rarely spoke. Customers came in, pointed at the bread they wanted, and Mr. Tani wrapped it without a single unnecessary word. Some neighbors thought he was cold. But those who watched him closely knew that his silence hid a warm heart.

Every morning at six, before the other shops opened, Mr. Tani left a paper bag of yesterday's unsold bread on the bench in front of the closed flower shop. He never told anyone, and he never put his name on it. The bag was simply there, and by seven it was always gone.

Aya, a fifteen-year-old student, noticed the bag one cold winter morning while waiting for her early bus. She watched an old man named Mr. Sato, who slept in the small park nearby because he had lost his home, take the bag quietly and walk away. Aya wanted to know who left the bread, so the next day she came even earlier and hid behind a vending machine. At five forty, she saw Mr. Tani place the bag on the bench and return to his shop without looking back. Aya said nothing, but from that day she began to greet him every morning.

Mr. Tani never responded with words. Still, Aya noticed small changes. One rainy day, she found a clean towel folded on the bakery counter, clearly placed there for her wet hair. Another day, when she mentioned she was hungry before a test, a warm roll appeared in her bag, though she had not bought it. She understood that Mr. Tani spoke through actions, not speech.

When spring came, the city announced a plan to widen the road, which meant the old shopping street would be torn down. Many shop owners decided to close and move away. Mr. Tani, however, said nothing about his plans. Aya was worried. If the bakery closed, what would happen to Mr. Sato, who still depended on the morning bread?

On the last day before the demolition began, Aya arrived early as always. The bench was empty. Her heart sank. But then she saw a new, larger paper bag, and beside it a small handwritten note — the first words she had ever seen from Mr. Tani. It read: "The bread will continue. New shop, two streets east. Tell our friend." Aya smiled and ran to the park to find Mr. Sato.

The corner bakery disappeared, but the quiet kindness did not. Mr. Tani had simply moved it, like he moved everything in his life, without asking for thanks.

Story Outline
- Setting: a small bakery at the entrance of an old shopping street
- Main character: Mr. Tani, a quiet baker who shows kindness through actions
- Other characters: Aya (a student), Mr. Sato (a homeless old man)
- Key events: [arranged in questions below]
- Theme: [explored in questions below]

question_data.passage:
You are an exchange student in Canada. In your English class, you read the following story written by a classmate and made notes to complete a Story Outline.

**My Coach, My Compass**

When I joined the school basketball team in my first year, I thought talent was everything. I had been the best player at my middle school, and I expected the same here. Our coach, Mr. Dawson, did not seem impressed. At my first practice, he watched me make a long, difficult shot and simply said, "Nice. Now do it ten times in a row." I missed seven of the next ten. He nodded as if that proved a point and walked away. I felt insulted. I had come to show what I could do, not to be corrected by a man in an old grey tracksuit.

For weeks, Mr. Dawson made the whole team repeat the same basic movements until they were boring. While other players practised exciting plays, he kept me passing the ball against a wall and catching it cleanly, again and again. One afternoon I complained loudly that this was a waste of my ability. He did not get angry. He only said quietly, "A house built on a weak floor falls in the first storm." I did not understand him then, and I was too proud to ask.

The storm came in our regional final. We were ahead by two points with seconds left when I received the ball under pressure. My hands, trained by all those hours against the wall, caught it cleanly without my thinking. I passed to an open teammate, who scored. We won. In the noise that followed, I looked for Mr. Dawson. He was not celebrating with the others. He stood at the side, arms folded, watching me with a small, satisfied smile, and then he gave a single nod—the same nod from my first practice.

Later that season, my closest teammate, Leah, broke her wrist and could not play. She came to every practice anyway, calling out advice and keeping our spirits up. I admired how she stayed part of the team even when she could not play. Mr. Dawson noticed her too. He quietly asked her to keep statistics and help plan our defence. "An injured player who still serves the team," he told me, "is worth more than a healthy one who only serves himself." Leah's notes later helped us beat a stronger rival.

At our final dinner, I expected Mr. Dawson to praise our victories. Instead, he spoke about effort, patience, and caring for one another. He never once mentioned the championship trophy on the table. When it was my turn to speak, I admitted that I had arrived believing I already knew everything, and that he had taught me how little I understood. He laughed warmly and said, "Now you are ready to learn." I realised that his hardest lessons had never been about basketball at all. They were about becoming a person worth following, the way I had come to follow him.

**Story Outline**

Main character: the narrator, a new and talented but proud team member
Key person 1: Mr. Dawson, the coach
Key person 2: Leah, an injured teammate

Theme of the story (to be decided)

You are in an English class. You are going to read the following story written by a high school student named Sora for a school magazine. After reading, you will organize the story by completing a "Story Outline."

**The Taste of Sunday**

When I was small, my grandmother Hana lived only two streets away from us. Every Sunday morning, my mother would send me to her house to deliver fresh vegetables from our garden. I always ran the whole way, because the moment I stepped through her door, the smell of warm soup would wrap around me like a blanket. Grandma Hana made a soup she called *imo-jiru*, a thick potato soup that no restaurant could ever copy. She never wrote the recipe down. "It lives in my hands," she would say, laughing, "not on paper."

For years I begged her to teach me, but she always gave the same answer: "When you are ready, the soup will tell you." I did not understand what she meant, and honestly, I thought she was just being mysterious. I was happy enough simply to eat it.

Everything changed the spring I turned fifteen. Grandma Hana fell ill and had to move into our house so my mother could care for her. She grew weaker each week, and the kitchen, once full of steam and the sound of chopping, went silent. One quiet evening she called me to her room. From under her pillow she took a small, worn notebook and pressed it into my hands. "I finally wrote it down," she whispered. "But the words are not enough. You must cook it yourself to learn the rest."

I opened the notebook that night. The recipe was there, but the handwriting was shaky and several lines were hard to read. I felt a sudden fear: what if I cooked it wrong? What if I lost her soup forever? I closed the notebook and did not open it again for a long time. I was afraid that my failure would somehow make her absence more real.

Grandma Hana passed away that summer. The notebook stayed in my desk drawer, untouched, for almost a year. Then, on the first Sunday of the following spring, my younger brother Riku, who was only seven, climbed onto a kitchen chair and asked me a question that I could not escape: "Sora, what did Grandma's soup taste like? I can't remember anymore." His words frightened me more than the recipe ever had. A memory was disappearing, and I held the only key to it.

That afternoon I took out the notebook. My hands shook as I peeled the potatoes, exactly as I had watched her do a hundred times. The first pot was a disaster—too salty, too thin. I tried again the next Sunday, and the next. Each week I adjusted one small thing. My mother would taste a spoonful, close her eyes, and say, "Closer. Keep going." Slowly, I began to understand what Grandma had meant. The recipe on paper was only a beginning; the real knowledge came from my own hands, from tasting and correcting and remembering.

On the seventh Sunday, Riku took one sip, looked up at me with wide eyes, and said, "That's it. That's Grandma's soup." I had to turn away so he would not see me cry.

Now I make *imo-jiru* every Sunday. Riku helps me peel the potatoes, and I tell him about the grandmother he barely knew. I finally understand her words. The soup did tell me when I was ready—not before I needed it, but exactly when our family needed to be reminded that she was still with us, in our hands and at our table.

Your team is reading a story written by a young office worker named Sora about her first months at a publishing company. Read the story and complete the Story Outline below.

The Quiet Desk

When Sora joined Marlow Press, she was sure she had made a mistake. The other new employees seemed to laugh easily and ask questions without fear, while she sat in silence, afraid that one wrong word would prove she did not belong. Her desk was at the far end of the room, next to a man named Mr. Okada, who had worked there for nearly twenty years. He rarely spoke. He drank black coffee, edited manuscripts with a red pen, and left at exactly six o'clock every day. Sora decided he must dislike her, and so she said nothing to him for two whole weeks.

One rainy Monday, Sora was given her first real task: to check a long manuscript for errors before it went to print. She worked late into the evening, certain she had done well. But the next morning, her supervisor returned the pages covered in corrections she had missed. Sora's face burned. She gathered the papers and hurried toward the stairwell, where no one could see her cry. To her surprise, Mr. Okada was already there, eating a sandwich alone. He looked at the papers in her hands and said only, "The first hundred mistakes are the cheapest ones you'll ever make. Make them now."

That afternoon, without being asked, Mr. Okada placed an old, worn notebook on her desk. Inside were pages of notes he had written when he was young, recording every error he had once made and how he had learned to catch it. "I kept this so I would not forget how it feels to be new," he said. Sora began copying his method, keeping her own list. Slowly, she stopped fearing mistakes and started hunting for them. Her corrections grew sharper. By spring, her supervisor praised her careful eye, and the other employees began asking her for advice.

Sora wanted to thank Mr. Okada, but he brushed away her words. "Don't thank me," he said. "When someone new sits beside you one day, give them the notebook." She did not fully understand him then. Months later, a nervous new employee named Kenji was seated at the desk on her other side. He made the same silent, frightened face she once had. Without thinking, Sora copied her notes into a fresh notebook and set it quietly on his desk. Mr. Okada, watching from across the room, gave a small nod and returned to his red pen. For the first time, Sora understood that kindness at work was not a gift to be repaid, but a habit to be passed on.

You are preparing for a school presentation about sleep and learning. You found the following article and made some slides.

Why Sleep Helps You Learn

Many students believe that the best way to remember new material is to keep studying late into the night. They cut their sleep short, thinking that more hours awake mean more hours of learning. Yet researchers who study the brain have found the opposite to be true. Sleep is not simply a pause in your day; it is an active period during which the brain organizes and strengthens what you learned while you were awake. Without enough of it, the effort you put into studying can quietly slip away.

To understand this, it helps to know how memory is formed. When you learn something new—a list of words, a math method, or a piece of music—your brain first stores it in a temporary, fragile form. At this early stage the memory is easily lost or confused with other information. The memory becomes stable only after it goes through a process called consolidation, in which the brain copies the information into longer-lasting storage and links it to things you already know. Studies show that a large share of consolidation happens during sleep, not during the busy hours of the day. This is why a fact you could barely recall at night may come back to you clearly the next morning.

Sleep is not all the same, however. During the night the brain moves through several stages again and again. One important stage is deep sleep, which tends to occur more in the first half of the night. Researchers believe that deep sleep is when the brain replays and files away facts and events—the kind of knowledge you need for a vocabulary test or a history exam. Another stage is dreaming sleep, often called REM sleep, which becomes longer toward the morning. REM sleep appears to help the brain connect ideas and recognize patterns, which supports problem-solving and creative thinking. Because these two stages do different jobs, losing sleep at either end of the night can harm a different kind of learning.

This points to a hidden danger in studying all night before a test. A student who stays awake until dawn may feel that the extra hours were well spent, but in fact the brain never gets the chance to file the new material away. In one experiment, students who slept after learning remembered far more the next day than students of equal ability who stayed awake the same length of time. The sleepers were not lazier or less hardworking; their advantage came entirely from giving the brain time to do its night work. The lesson is clear: an hour of sleep after studying can be worth more than an extra hour of cramming.

Naps can help too, but timing matters. A short nap of about twenty minutes can refresh attention and lift mood without leaving you groggy. A longer nap, especially one that reaches deep sleep, can also support memory, but waking from deep sleep often leaves a heavy, foggy feeling that can last half an hour. For this reason, a brief nap in the early afternoon is usually the safest choice for a busy student.

What does all this mean for your study habits? First, treat sleep as part of studying, not as time stolen from it. Second, try to learn the most important material earlier in the evening, then protect a full night's sleep so that both deep sleep and REM sleep can do their work. Finally, keep a regular schedule, since a brain that knows when sleep is coming makes better use of it. Working with your sleep, rather than against it, may be the simplest way to learn more from the same amount of effort.

You are preparing for a presentation in your English class. You have read the following passage and are going to make slides to summarize it.

How Music Shapes the Brain and Mood

Almost everyone listens to music, but few people stop to ask why a favorite song can lift a tired spirit or calm a nervous mind. Over the past twenty years, scientists who study the brain have begun to explain what happens inside us when we hear music. Their findings suggest that music is far more than simple entertainment. It can change how we feel, help us focus, and even support our health.

When we listen to a song we love, the brain releases a chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is the same substance that gives us pleasure when we eat good food or receive praise. Interestingly, researchers have found that the strongest release of dopamine does not come at the exact moment a thrilling part of the music arrives. Instead, it comes in the seconds just before that moment, while the brain is predicting what will happen next. In other words, the pleasure of music depends partly on expectation. A song that is completely predictable becomes boring, while a song that is totally strange gives the brain nothing to predict. The music we enjoy most usually sits between these two extremes, mixing the familiar with a few surprises.

Music also affects the body in measurable ways. Slow, gentle music with about sixty beats per minute can cause the heart to beat more slowly and the muscles to relax. In one experiment, patients who listened to calm music before surgery felt less anxious than patients who took common anti-anxiety medicine. Fast music with a strong rhythm has the opposite effect: it raises energy and can make exercise feel easier. Some runners report that they can run longer when they match their steps to an upbeat song, because the rhythm seems to hide their feeling of tiredness.

The benefits of music are not limited to single moments. Learning to play an instrument changes the brain over a long period. When children practice an instrument for several years, the parts of the brain that control movement, hearing, and memory grow stronger and work together more smoothly. These changes appear to help with skills that have nothing to do with music, such as reading and solving math problems. However, scientists are careful here. They point out that musical training and academic ability often appear together, but this does not prove that one directly causes the other. Families who support music lessons may also support study in other ways.

Music can heal as well as please. In hospitals, trained music therapists use songs and rhythms to help patients recover. People who have lost the ability to speak after a brain injury can sometimes sing words they cannot say, and by practicing through song, a few slowly regain ordinary speech. For older people with memory loss, a familiar tune from their youth can suddenly bring back names, places, and feelings that seemed gone forever. This happens because musical memories are stored widely across the brain, so they often survive even when other memories fade.

Given all this, how should we use music in daily life? Researchers offer simple advice. Choose calm, slow music when you need to relax or sleep, and save energetic music for exercise or boring tasks. Be aware that music with words can disturb activities that also use language, such as writing or reading, so silence or wordless music may be better at those times. Above all, make room for the songs you truly love, because the music that moves you the most is also the music most likely to do you good.

You are preparing a presentation for your English class based on the following article about how habits are formed.

How Habits Take Shape

Most of us repeat dozens of small actions every day without thinking about them. We brush our teeth, check our phones, or pour a cup of coffee almost automatically. These automatic actions are called habits, and scientists who study the brain say that understanding how they form can help us build good ones and break bad ones.

A habit develops through a simple three-part cycle that researchers call the "habit loop." First comes a cue, which is a signal that tells the brain to start a certain action. A cue can be a time of day, a place, an emotion, or even another action you have just finished. Second comes the routine, which is the action itself, such as eating a snack or going for a run. Third comes the reward, which is the good feeling or benefit you get afterward. The brain remembers that the routine produced something pleasant, so the next time the same cue appears, it pushes you to repeat the routine. Importantly, a habit only takes hold when all three parts are linked together. If a routine brings no reward, the brain has no reason to store it, and the behavior does not become automatic.

Repetition is what turns this loop into a lasting habit. Each time the cue, routine, and reward occur in order, the connection between them grows stronger inside the brain. After enough repetitions, the brain begins to expect the reward as soon as it notices the cue. At that point, the action starts to feel almost effortless, and you may carry it out before you are even aware of deciding to. This is why old habits are hard to change: the brain runs them in the background to save energy, leaving your conscious mind free for other tasks.

One common question is how long it takes to form a new habit. A well-known study followed volunteers who tried to adopt a new daily action, such as drinking water at lunch or walking after dinner. The researchers found that the time needed varied widely from person to person, ranging from about three weeks to several months. On average, it took around ten weeks before an action felt automatic. The study also showed that missing the action on a single day did not ruin the process. What mattered most was keeping the action tied to the same cue and repeating it as regularly as possible over time.

Knowing how the habit loop works, experts offer practical advice for building better habits. They suggest attaching a new routine to a cue that already exists in your day, such as doing ten minutes of study right after you finish breakfast. This makes the cue easy to notice and hard to forget. They also recommend choosing a small, clear reward to enjoy right after the routine, because an immediate reward strengthens the loop far better than a distant one. Finally, they advise being patient and not giving up after an occasional missed day, since regular repetition over many weeks matters more than being perfect every single day.

You are studying how the brain learns. You found an English article and made slides to present its main points.

[Article]

Why Curiosity Helps Us Learn

Have you ever noticed how easily you remember the answer to a question that you truly wanted to know? Scientists have long suspected that curiosity—the feeling of wanting to find out something—does more than make learning enjoyable. Recent studies of the brain now show that curiosity actually changes how well the brain takes in and stores new information.

In one well-known experiment, researchers showed volunteers a long list of trivia questions, such as "What does the word 'dinosaur' actually mean?" Before seeing each answer, the volunteers rated how curious they were to learn it. The researchers scanned the volunteers' brains while they waited for each answer to appear. The waiting period was important: it was the gap between reading a question and seeing its answer that revealed the strongest effects. When people felt highly curious, two things happened in the brain. First, areas linked to reward and pleasure became more active, the same areas that respond to things people enjoy, such as food or music. Second, a region called the hippocampus, which is essential for forming lasting memories, also became more active. In other words, a curious brain prepares itself to absorb knowledge even before the new information arrives.

This preparation produces clear results. A day later, the volunteers were tested on the answers. They remembered far more of the answers to questions they had been curious about than the answers they had felt little interest in. The size of the difference surprised the researchers. Curiosity, it seemed, acted like an open door, allowing facts to enter and stay in memory.

Perhaps the most striking finding was an unexpected side effect. During the waiting period after a question that made them curious, the volunteers were also briefly shown a photograph of a face that had nothing to do with the trivia. These faces were not interesting in themselves, and the volunteers were not told to remember them. Yet when curiosity was high, people later recalled these unrelated faces better, too. This suggests that once curiosity switches the brain into a learning-ready state, that state spreads. Information that happens to arrive at the same moment is also captured more firmly—even material the learner never meant to study.

Why does this happen? Researchers point to a brain chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is often described as the "reward" chemical, but it does more than create pleasant feelings. It also strengthens the connections between brain cells that store memories. When curiosity rises, the brain releases more dopamine, and this rise appears to support the hippocampus as it locks in new memories. The pleasant feeling of curiosity and the improvement in memory therefore share a single underlying cause.

These findings carry a practical message for anyone who wants to learn. Simply forcing yourself to memorize facts is not the most effective path. Instead, it helps to first stir up a genuine question in your mind—to wonder about the topic before studying it. A teacher who opens a lesson with a puzzling question, or a student who pauses to ask "Why is this true?" before reading a textbook, may be doing more than adding interest. They may be switching the brain into a state in which learning of all kinds comes more easily. Curiosity, the research suggests, is not a luxury for learning. It is one of its engines.
