question_data.passage:
You are preparing a presentation for your English class about a recent science article. Read the passage and complete the slides.

Why We Forget: The Hidden Work of a Healthy Mind

Many people treat forgetting as a kind of failure. When we cannot recall a name, a date, or where we left our keys, we often feel that our brain has let us down. Scientists, however, are now telling a very different story. According to recent research in memory science, forgetting is not simply the breakdown of memory. In many cases, it is an active and useful process that helps the brain work better. In other words, a brain that forgets well is often a brain that thinks well.

To understand this, it helps to know how memories are stored. When you experience something, groups of brain cells called neurons connect with one another and form a pattern. Each time you recall the experience, that same pattern becomes active again, and the connection grows a little stronger. This is why repeated practice helps you remember. But the brain receives far more information every day than it could ever need. If every detail stayed equally strong forever, useful memories would be buried under a mountain of unimportant ones. Forgetting solves this problem. By letting weak or rarely used connections fade, the brain keeps the information that matters most easy to find.

Researchers describe two main ways that forgetting happens. The first is natural fading. A memory that is not used for a long time slowly weakens, much as a path through a forest disappears when no one walks on it. The second is active removal. During deep sleep, the brain reviews the day's experiences and decides which connections to keep and which to weaken on purpose. Far from being lazy, the sleeping brain is busy cleaning house. This is one reason scientists say that a good night's sleep does not only rest the mind; it also shapes what the mind will remember.

Forgetting also supports clear thinking in everyday life. Imagine trying to remember where your car is parked today. If you could perfectly recall every parking spot you have ever used, those old memories would compete with today's, and you might walk to the wrong place. By weakening yesterday's details, the brain reduces this kind of confusion and lets the most recent and relevant information come to mind first. In this sense, forgetting is not the enemy of memory but its partner.

There may be an emotional benefit as well. Studies suggest that, over time, the sharp pain of a bad experience tends to fade faster than the pleasant feeling of a good one. Because of this gentle forgetting, many people remember their past more positively than it actually was. This does not mean we forget serious events, but the small daily annoyances usually lose their power. A mind that held on to every disappointment with full strength would find it much harder to stay hopeful.

Knowing all this, we can treat our own forgetting with less worry. Sleeping enough gives the brain the time it needs to sort memories. Reviewing important material more than once, with breaks in between, strengthens the connections we want to keep. And accepting that some details will slip away allows us to focus our limited attention on what truly matters. Forgetting, it turns out, is not a sign that the mind is failing. It is one of the quiet ways a healthy mind keeps itself in good working order.

Presentation Slides (draft)

Slide 1: Title
- Why We Forget: A Useful Skill of the Brain

Slide 2: A New View of Forgetting
- Old idea: forgetting = ( A )
- New idea: forgetting can help the brain

Slide 3: How Forgetting Helps
- ( B )
- ( C )

Slide 4: Two Ways Forgetting Happens
- 1. Natural fading
- 2. Active removal during ( D )

Slide 5: Advice for a Healthy Memory
- Sleep enough
- Review important things, with breaks
- Stop worrying about small forgotten details

Your English class is preparing a small magazine. As part of a writing project, your group is studying how social media affects people's connections and their ability to focus. Each member has written a short comment, and you have also collected two sources to support the discussion.

Comments from group members:

Hana: I joined social media to keep in touch with my old friends after we moved to different high schools. It really works for that. Last month I saw that a friend from my old town was visiting my city, and we met for the first time in two years. Without the app, I would never have known she was nearby. So I think these tools genuinely help us hold on to relationships that distance would otherwise break. The problem is not the connection itself; it is how often we check.

Kenji: I agree that staying connected is valuable, but I have noticed something about my own studying. When my phone is on my desk, I unlock it again and again without deciding to. Even after I put it in another room, my mind keeps wondering what messages I might be missing. I am not saying social media is bad for friendship. I am saying it quietly steals the attention I need for deep work, and I only realized this after tracking my own habits for two weeks.

Mei: For me the real worry is the comparison. When I scroll, I see only the best moments of everyone's lives, and I start to feel that my own ordinary days are not enough. I still message my close friends and that part is fine, but the endless stream of polished photos leaves me feeling more alone, not less. So I would not say the tools simply bring us together. They can also push us apart from how we feel about ourselves.

Taro: I run a club account, and honestly social media is the only reason our small club survived. We post about events and new students find us. People who were too shy to speak to us in person send messages first, and then come to a meeting. For students who feel left out at school, an online door can be easier to open than a real one. The focus problem is real, but I think we blame the tool when the habit is ours to manage.

Source A (a short article):
A psychologist writing for a student newspaper explained that the human brain treats a buzzing or flashing phone as a small reward to be chased. Each notification, she wrote, pulls attention away from whatever task is in front of us, and returning fully to that task can take several minutes. The danger, she argued, is not a single interruption but the steady habit of switching, which trains the mind to crave new input and makes long, uninterrupted thinking feel uncomfortable. She added that turning off notifications, rather than relying on willpower, is the most reliable fix, because it removes the trigger instead of fighting it.

Source B (results of a survey of 600 students at one high school):
Students were asked about their experiences with social media. The results below show the percentage who agreed with each statement.

- "Social media helps me stay in touch with friends I rarely see in person": 71%
- "I check my phone without meaning to while studying": 64%
- "I sometimes feel worse about my own life after using social media": 49%
- "I have made a new friend or joined a group through social media": 38%
- "I would find it hard to concentrate even if my phone were in another room": 52%

Your high school English class is preparing a short essay project on the question: "Should schools encourage students to use AI tools for studying?" Below are comments from four classmates, followed by two sources you collected for support.

**Comments from classmates**

Hana: I started using an AI study app last term, and it changed how I learn. When I get stuck on a math problem at night, I can ask the app and it explains each step until I understand. My teacher cannot answer my questions at midnight, but the app can. I used to give up on hard homework, but now I keep going because help is always there. For me, the biggest benefit is that AI removes the fear of getting stuck alone.

Kenji: I agree that AI can help, but I worry about one thing. When the app gives the full answer right away, some of my friends just copy it without thinking. They feel they have studied, but on the test they cannot solve anything. The problem is not the tool itself; it is how people use it. If AI only shows the final answer, it makes students lazy. Schools should teach students to use it as a guide, not as a machine that does the work for them.

Mei: My view is different. I think the danger is that students stop trusting their own thinking. Last month, my AI tutor confidently gave me a wrong explanation in history, and I believed it until my teacher corrected me. AI sounds sure even when it is mistaken, so younger students may not notice the errors. A human teacher knows when I am confused by my face; an app does not. I am not against AI, but I believe schools should keep teachers at the center.

Riku: I focus on fairness. Good AI tutoring apps often cost money, and a fast internet connection is not free either. If schools recommend these tools, students from richer families will get even more support, while others fall behind. In the past, everyone had the same textbook. Now, the gap may grow. So before we encourage AI, schools should make sure every student can actually use it equally.

**Source A (from a school newsletter)**

A teacher at our school ran a four-week experiment with two groups of first-year students. Group 1 used an AI app that gave full answers immediately. Group 2 used an AI app set to give only hints and questions, never the final answer. Both groups studied the same topics for the same number of hours. At the end, Group 2 scored higher on a problem-solving test and, more importantly, could explain their reasoning out loud. The teacher concluded that AI helps most when it is designed to make students think, not when it simply hands over answers.

**Source B (results of a survey of 300 students at our school)**

Students were asked which statements describe their own experience with AI study tools. The percentages who agreed were:

- "I understand difficult topics faster with AI help": all students 71%, students who own a paid app 88%, students with no paid app 49%
- "I sometimes accept AI answers without checking them": all students 64%
- "I can study at any time, even late at night": all students 80%
- "I feel I rely on AI too much": all students 45%

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes Kenji's opinion?

questions.stem: Based on Source A, which statement is best supported?
choices: AI apps are equally effective no matter how they are designed.

questions.explanation: 正解は「Students learn problem-solving better when the AI gives hints and questions instead of full answers.」。Source Aでは、ヒントと問いだけを返す設定のGroup 2が問題解決テストで高得点を取り、理由を口頭で説明できたとあり、教員は「AI helps most when it is designed to make students think」と結論づける。両群は同じ時間学習したので学習時間差は無関係(選択肢2)。設計で結果が変わったのだから「設計に関係なく同等」(選択肢3)は誤り。理由を説明できたのはGroup 2であってGroup 1ではない(選択肢4は人物の取り違え)。

questions.stem: Hana claims that AI's greatest value is that students can get help at any time and therefore keep studying. Which result from Source B most strongly supports her claim?
choices: 64% of all students sometimes accept AI answers without checking them.
Among students with no paid app, only 49% understand difficult topics faster with AI help.
45% of all students feel they rely on AI too much.
80% of all students agreed that they can study at any time, even late at night.
questions.explanation: 正解は「80% of all students agreed that they can study at any time, even late at night.」。Hanaの主張の核心は「いつでも(深夜でも)助けが得られるので学習を続けられる」という点で、Source Bの「I can study at any time, even late at night: all students 80%」がこれを最も強く裏づける。64%の無確認受容(選択肢1)やAIへの過度の依存45%(選択肢3)はむしろ懸念を示す数値で主張を支えない。選択肢4は有料アプリ非所有者の理解度の話で、公平性(Riku)の論点であり「常時利用できる」という主張の根拠ではない。

Your English class is preparing essays on the topic "Should single-use plastics be banned?" Your teacher has asked everyone to read four classmates' comments and two sources before writing.

[Comments from classmates]

Maya: I strongly believe that single-use plastics, such as straws, bags, and food containers, should be banned completely. Last summer I volunteered to clean a beach near my house, and I was shocked to find hundreds of plastic bottles and broken bags buried in the sand. Animals can mistake these pieces for food and die. Some people say plastic is convenient, but I think our convenience should never come before the health of the ocean. A full ban would force companies to find better materials, and I am sure they could do it if the law required them to.

Daniel: I understand why people worry about pollution, but I do not think a complete ban is the right answer. Plastic is cheap, light, and very useful in hospitals and for keeping food fresh, which reduces food waste. The real problem is not plastic itself but the way we throw it away. If every town built a good recycling system and people learned to use the bins correctly, most of the harm would disappear. We should fix our habits, not ban a useful material.

Sophia: When I was younger, my family relied on cheap plastic bottles because we could not always afford other options. A sudden ban would hurt low-income families the most, because the alternatives, like glass or metal, often cost more. I agree that pollution is a serious issue, but any new rule must be fair. I would support a gradual change that gives people time and affordable choices, rather than a law that punishes those who have the least money.

Ken: To me, the most important question is whether a policy actually changes behavior. Banning straws feels good, but straws are only a tiny part of the plastic in the sea. If we ban one small item and feel satisfied, we may ignore the bigger sources of waste. I would rather see governments charge a fee on all plastic packaging. People notice when something costs more, and a fee would push both companies and shoppers to cut back across the board, not just on one product.

[Source A: a short news article]

A coastal town in northern Europe introduced a small fee on every plastic shopping bag two years ago. Shops kept the same bags on their shelves, but each one now cost a few extra coins. The town did not ban anything; customers were still free to buy plastic bags if they wished. Within a year, the number of plastic bags used in the town fell by almost half, as many shoppers simply brought their own reusable bags. Town officials reported that complaints from residents were rare, and most shops said the change was easy to manage. However, officials also noted that the use of other plastic items, such as food wrap and bottles, stayed almost the same, because the fee applied only to bags.

[Source B: a survey of 1,000 residents]

Residents were asked whether they agreed with different plastic policies. The results were as follows:
- Support a small fee on plastic bags: 78%
- Support a complete ban on all single-use plastics: 41%
- Worried that a ban would raise their living costs: 63%
- Already bring a reusable bag when shopping: 52%
- Believe better recycling is more important than a ban: 69%

A ban would be unfair because alternatives cost too much for poor families.
A fee on all plastic packaging would change people's behavior most effectively.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Plastic is useful, so the focus should be on disposal and recycling rather than a ban.」。Danielは「I do not think a complete ban is the right answer」「The real problem is not plastic itself but the way we throw it away」「We should fix our habits, not ban a useful material」と述べ、禁止ではなく廃棄・リサイクルの改善を主張している。選択肢1はMaya、2はSophia、3はKenの意見。

questions.stem: Maya and Ken would most likely agree that
choices: a complete ban on all single-use plastics is the only acceptable solution.
the current amount of plastic harming the environment is a serious problem that requires action.
charging a fee on plastic packaging is better than banning any single item.
low-income families should be protected from any rise in living costs.
questions.explanation: 正解は「the current amount of plastic harming the environment is a serious problem that requires action.」。Mayaはビーチでの体験から海洋汚染を深刻視し行動(全面禁止)を求め、Kenも「straws are only a tiny part of the plastic in the sea」と認めつつ料金制という行動を提案している。両者とも「対策が必要な深刻な問題」という点で一致する。選択肢1はMayaのみ、3はKenのみ、4はSophiaの主張。

questions.stem: Which classmate's opinion is most strongly supported by Source A?
choices: Maya
Sophia
Daniel
Ken
questions.explanation: 正解は「Ken」。Kenは禁止より「charge a fee on all plastic packaging」を支持し、料金が人々の行動を変えると主張する。Source Aでは、禁止せず袋に少額の料金を課しただけで使用量が約半分に減り、人々がエコバッグを持参するようになったと報告されており、まさに料金制が行動を変えるというKenの立場を裏付ける。

questions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the survey data in Source B?
choices: More residents support a complete ban on single-use plastics than support a fee on plastic bags.
Most residents believe a ban is more important than improving recycling.
A clear majority of residents are concerned that a ban could increase their cost of living.
Fewer than half of the residents already bring a reusable bag when shopping.
questions.explanation: 正解は「A clear majority of residents are concerned that a ban could increase their cost of living.」。Source Bで「Worried that a ban would raise their living costs: 63%」と過半数を超える。選択肢1は誤り(料金支持78% > 全面禁止支持41%)。選択肢3も誤り(リサイクルの方が重要69% > 禁止)。選択肢4も誤り(エコバッグ持参は52%で半数超)。

question_data.passage:
Your English class is preparing a small magazine on the theme "Should companies let employees work from home?" Four students wrote short opinions, and your teacher added two sources. Read them and complete the tasks.

Mika: I worked from home during a school project with my older sister, who is a software engineer, and I saw how much it helped her. She no longer spends two hours on crowded trains every day, so she starts work feeling calm and finishes her tasks faster. She told me that on days when she goes to the office, she is already tired before lunch. Companies should trust their workers and let them choose where they work best. People who are not forced to travel can use that time for sleep, family, or learning new skills.

Daniel: I agree that travelling less is good, but I worry about young workers. When my cousin started his first job fully from home, no one taught him the small things—how to write a polite email, how to ask for help, how to behave in a meeting. He felt lonely and almost quit. Older workers already have these skills, so home may suit them, but beginners need to sit near experienced people and watch how they work. Without that, they grow slowly and lose confidence.

Saki: For me the real problem is fairness. Not every home is a good office. My family lives in a small apartment, and my mother, who is an accountant, has no quiet room. She works at the kitchen table while my little brother plays nearby, so she cannot concentrate. Meanwhile, my friend's mother has a private study and loves working from home. If companies send everyone home, they help people with big houses and hurt people without them. The office, at least, gives everyone the same conditions.

Ren: I think the answer is a mix. My aunt's company lets staff come to the office two or three days a week and work from home the rest. On office days, the team meets, shares ideas, and trains new members. On home days, people do quiet tasks that need deep focus. My aunt says this plan keeps both the human connection and the freedom. Choosing only one side—all office or all home—throws away the good points of the other.

Source A (from a business magazine): A study followed one company that moved its sales team fully to remote work for a year. The total number of completed sales reports rose by 13 percent, because workers wasted less time travelling and could plan their own hours. However, the company also found that new employees hired during that year took almost twice as long to reach the same skill level as new employees from earlier years. Managers said the older, experienced staff did well alone, but beginners struggled because they had few chances to watch and copy skilled colleagues nearby.

Source B (from a national survey of office workers): Workers were asked, "Do you feel you can concentrate well where you work?" The results, sorted by home situation, were as follows:
- Workers with a private room at home: 81 percent said yes.
- Workers without a private room at home: 48 percent said yes.
- All workers when at the company office: 72 percent said yes.
Workers were also asked whether they wanted to return to the office full-time. Only 19 percent said yes.
question_data.subject: 英語

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Saki's main opinion?
choices: A combination of office days and home days keeps both connection and freedom.
Working from home is good because it removes the stress of daily commuting.
Young workers should stay in the office so that experienced staff can train them.
Working from home is unfair because it benefits only those who have suitable space at home.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Working from home is unfair because it benefits only those who have suitable space at home.」。Sakiは「the real problem is fairness」と述べ、狭いアパートで集中できない母親と、専用書斎を持つ友人の母親を対比し、在宅にすると「help people with big houses and hurt people without them」と論じている。通勤の話はMika、若手育成はDaniel、混合案はRenの意見であり混同。

questions.stem: Which two students would most likely agree that employees who must work entirely from home can have serious problems?
choices: Mika and Ren
Daniel and Saki
Mika and Daniel
Saki and Ren
questions.explanation: 正解は「Daniel and Saki」。Danielは完全在宅だと若手が小さなマナーを学べず孤独で「almost quit」になると問題視し、Sakiは家に静かな部屋がない人は集中できず不公平だと述べる。両者とも「全員を家に送る」ことの深刻な弊害を指摘している。Mikaは在宅を強く支持、Renは混合案で、完全在宅そのものの害を中心には論じていない。

questions.stem: Whose opinion does Ren's idea most directly try to combine?
choices: Mika's view that workers should be free from commuting, and Daniel's view that beginners need experienced people nearby.
Saki's view about unfair housing, and Source B's survey numbers.
Daniel's view about loneliness, and Saki's view about kitchen tables.
Mika's view about trust, and Saki's view that the office gives equal conditions.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Mika's view that workers should be free from commuting, and Daniel's view that beginners need experienced people nearby.」。Renの混合案は「home days」で集中作業の自由(Mikaの通勤からの解放に通じる)を保ちつつ、「office days」でチームが新人を訓練する(Danielの「beginners need to sit near experienced people」)。両者の長所を取り込もうとしており、「Choosing only one side ... throws away the good points of the other」と述べる。

questions.stem: According to Source A, which statement is best supported?
choices: Both experienced and new workers improved equally under remote work.
Remote work lowered the number of sales reports but helped new workers grow faster.
Remote work raised output but slowed the growth of newly hired workers.
Remote work failed because experienced staff could not work alone.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Remote work raised output but slowed the growth of newly hired workers.」。Source Aは完成した営業報告が「rose by 13 percent」と生産が上がった一方、その年の新入社員は以前の新人の「almost twice as long」かけて同じ技能水準に達したと述べる。経験者はうまくいったが新人が伸び悩んだという内容で、他の選択肢は数値や因果を取り違えている。

questions.stem: Using the numbers in Source B, which conclusion is most clearly supported?
choices: Workers without a private room concentrate just as well as those with one.
Having a private room at home makes a large difference in whether workers feel they can concentrate.
Most workers want to go back to the office full-time.
Workers concentrate better in the office than anywhere at home.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Having a private room at home makes a large difference in whether workers feel they can concentrate.」。Source Bでは専用部屋がある人の81%が集中できると答えたのに対し、ない人は48%で、その差は大きい。全社員のオフィスでの数値72%は専用部屋なし(48%)より高いが専用部屋あり(81%)より低いので「家のどこより上」は誤り。フルタイム復帰希望は19%のみなので「大半が戻りたい」も誤り。

question_data.passage:
Your English class is preparing essays on the theme "Tourism and Local Culture." Read the four students' opinions and the two sources below, and answer the questions that follow.

**Mika:** I grew up in a small mountain town that almost no one visited ten years ago. Now, thousands of travelers come every autumn to see the colored leaves. The visitors spend money at our shops and restaurants, so several closed stores have reopened, and three of my old classmates moved back to run a café and a guesthouse. Without tourism, our young people would have left forever. To me, the most important thing is that the town is alive again, even if the streets are sometimes crowded.

**Daniel:** I understand that tourism brings money, but I worry about what it does to a culture. In the old town where I live, the local craft shops that made pottery and woven baskets have been replaced by stores selling cheap key rings and the same T-shirts you can buy anywhere. The festivals that were once for the community are now performed mainly for cameras. Money is flowing in, yet what makes our town special is quietly disappearing. We should protect the real culture, not turn it into a show.

**Sora:** Both sides have a point, but the real question is who decides. In many places, big outside companies build the hotels and keep most of the profit, while local people only get low-paying jobs and rising rents. I believe tourism can be good, but only when the community itself controls it. If residents own the businesses and set the rules, the benefits stay local and the culture is respected. Otherwise, we are just selling our home to strangers.

**Emma:** I think we worry too much. Travel lets people from different countries meet and learn from one another. When I visited my grandparents' village, tourists asked me about our customs, and I felt proud to explain them. Sharing our culture with the world is not the same as losing it. As long as we keep teaching the meaning behind our traditions to the next generation, a few souvenir shops will not erase who we are.

**Source A (newspaper article):**
Last year, the historic district of Riverton introduced a "community tourism" rule. Any new hotel or restaurant must be at least half-owned by local residents, and a small share of every visitor's spending goes into a town fund. The fund has already paid to repair an old theater and to train young people in traditional weaving. The mayor reported that, unlike in nearby towns where outside firms dominate, most of Riverton's tourism income now stays in the community, and complaints about rising rents have fallen sharply. Several residents who had moved away have returned to open family businesses.

**Source B (survey data):**
A survey asked 500 residents of tourist towns whether they agreed that "tourism has improved life in my town." Results are shown by the type of town:
- Towns where most businesses are locally owned: 71% agreed, 18% disagreed, 11% unsure.
- Towns where most businesses are owned by outside companies: 34% agreed, 52% disagreed, 14% unsure.
- Towns with very few tourists: 40% agreed, 25% disagreed, 35% unsure.
The survey also found that in locally owned towns, 66% said local traditions were "well preserved," while in outside-owned towns only 29% said so.
question_data.subject: 英語

questions.stem: What is Daniel's main point?
choices: Tourism should be stopped because it never brings any money to small towns.
Local people should sell more T-shirts and key rings to earn money from visitors.
The income from tourism is causing the town's genuine culture to fade as authentic crafts and community festivals are replaced by commercial imitations.
Festivals are better when they are performed for tourists with cameras.
questions.explanation: 正解は「The income from tourism is causing the town's genuine culture to fade as authentic crafts and community festivals are replaced by commercial imitations.」。Danielは「Money is flowing in, yet what makes our town special is quietly disappearing」と述べ、陶器やかご作りの工芸店が安価な土産物店に置き換わり、地域の祭りがカメラ向けの見せ物になったと指摘している。お金は入っても本物の文化が消える点を問題視しており、観光を完全に止めよとは言っていない。

questions.stem: Which opinion is shared by both Mika and Emma?
choices: Tourism should be controlled only by local residents who own the businesses.
The arrival of tourists has, on balance, a positive effect and need not be feared.
Souvenir shops are destroying the identity of every town they appear in.
Outside companies take most of the profit and leave locals with low-paying jobs.
questions.explanation: 正解は「The arrival of tourists has, on balance, a positive effect and need not be feared.」。Mikaは観光で町が再び活気づき若者が戻ったことを「the town is alive again」と肯定し、Emmaは「I think we worry too much」「a few souvenir shops will not erase who we are」と述べて観光を前向きに評価している。両者とも観光の利点を強調し過度な心配を退ける点で共通する。選択肢1はSora、4もSoraの主張で、3はどちらも述べていない。

questions.stem: Whose opinions are most directly supported by Source A?
choices: Daniel and Emma
Mika and Daniel
Emma and Sora
Sora and Mika
questions.explanation: 正解は「Sora and Mika」。Source Aのリバートンは、新規ホテル・飲食店を住民が半分以上所有することを義務づけ、観光収入が地域に残るようにした例で、「コミュニティが観光を管理してこそ利益が地元に残る」というSoraの主張を裏づける。また町を出ていた住民が戻り家業を始めた点は、観光で町が再生し仲間が戻ったというMikaの経験と一致する。Danielの懸念(文化の商業化)やEmmaの文化共有論を直接支持する記述はSource Aにない。

questions.stem: According to Source A, what is one specific result of Riverton's "community tourism" rule?
choices: Outside firms came to own most of the town's new hotels.
Rents in Riverton rose faster than in nearby towns.
The number of tourists visiting Riverton fell sharply.
A town fund financed the repair of an old theater and the training of young weavers.
questions.explanation: 正解は「A town fund financed the repair of an old theater and the training of young weavers.」。Source Aは「The fund has already paid to repair an old theater and to train young people in traditional weaving」と明記している。ルールにより外部企業が支配する近隣町とは異なり収入が地域に残り、家賃上昇への不満はむしろ減った(fallen sharply)ので、選択肢1・4は本文と矛盾する。観光客数の減少には言及がない。

questions.stem: Based on the data in Source B, which statement is best supported?
choices: In outside-owned towns, more residents disagreed than agreed that tourism had improved life, and fewer felt their traditions were well preserved than in locally owned towns.
Residents of towns with very few tourists agreed most strongly that tourism had improved their lives.
Local ownership made no difference to how residents viewed tourism.
In locally owned towns, most residents felt their traditions were poorly preserved.
questions.explanation: 正解は「In outside-owned towns, more residents disagreed than agreed that tourism had improved life, and fewer felt their traditions were well preserved than in locally owned towns.」。Source Bでは外部所有の町で「agreed 34%・disagreed 52%」と不同意が同意を上回り、伝統が「well preserved」と答えた割合も外部所有29%に対し地元所有66%と低い。選択肢1は観光が少ない町の同意40%が地元所有71%より低いので誤り、3は数値差が大きく誤り、4は地元所有で66%が良好と答えており誤り。
